pull_requests.title: Add XComIterable.flatten() to read an iterated task's pages as one sequence
pull_requests.body:
> **Review only this change:** [the PR's own commit](https://github.com/apache/airflow/pull/73807/commits/c06e3cbbc3b9f6ed0e03ddab5301dbe2ee67b5fb) · [diff against #62922's branch](https://github.com/dabla/airflow/compare/feature/dynamic-task-iteration...feature/xcom-iterable-flatten). Everything else in this PR's commit list and file list is #62922, which this PR is stacked on.

Stacked on #62922 (Task Iteration): only the last commit, c06e3cbbc3, belongs to this PR. It will be rebased once #62922 merges.

related: #62922

## What

An iterated task whose iterations each return a page of items, for example one list of rows per API call, pushes one XCom per iteration and returns the `XComIterable` over them. `.flatten()` on that output gives a downstream task those pages as one `Sequence` of items:

```python
pages = fetch_page.iterate(page=range(10))  # each iteration returns a list of rows
load_rows(pages.output.flatten())  # one sequence of rows, page boundaries gone
```

Nested lists, tuples and sets are expanded recursively; strings, bytes and scalars stay single items.

## How

- `FlattenedXComIterable` speaks in flattened positions. Its length is the `flattened_length` that `IterableOperator.axcom_push` tallies from each value as it is pushed, while the value is in memory, so the view knows its length without reading a page. An `XComIterable` pushed without the tally is counted by reading its pages once.
- Reads hold the last page fetched and nothing more: a sequential read (iteration, a slice, an iterated task consuming this as its input) fetches every page exactly once, a read within the held page costs nothing, and a jump backwards restarts from the first page. Memory stays bounded by one page.
- The same cursor serves `__getitem__`/`__iter__` (blocking reads) and `aget`/`__aiter__` (reads through `asend`, safe on the task's event loop).

## Why a separate PR

This was part of #62922, but task iteration does not need it: nothing in the SDK outside `bases/xcom.py` referred to it, and it had no documentation there. Splitting it out keeps #62922 about running a task over its input, and gives flatten its own review and its own paragraph in the task-sdk docs, included here.

## Tests

`test_xcom.py` covers expansion of lists, tuples, sets, generators and mixed pages, string/bytes/scalar pass-through, negative indices on both paths, the tallied length round-tripping through serde, one page read per page on a sequential read, the no-tally counting pass, and the one-page memory bound. `test_serde.py` round-trips the flattened view.

pull_requests.title: Enforce execution_timeout from the task supervisor side
pull_requests.body:
Exact same work in #72493. Created this because that one was closed by the PR number limit policy.

## Why

`execution_timeout` is only enforced by a SIGALRM handler inside the task runner process. When that process is stuck in native code or hit by SIGSEGV, the handler never runs and the task stays running forever (#57174, #57712, #45930).

To tackle the problem at its root, the better solution is to handle the runner's timeout from the supervisor side.

## What

The task process sends a new `SetExecutionTimeout` message to the supervisor right before it arms its own alarm, so both clocks start at the same point. If the task has not reported a terminal state within 5 seconds after the timeout, the supervisor sends SIGTERM to the process group, and SIGKILL 5 seconds later.

This keeps the task runner's SIGALRM handler instead of "moving it", which is a bit different from what #53337 asks for. The reason is that `on_kill`, the retry policy and the failure callbacks can only run inside the task process, and dropping the handler would skip them on every timeout.

closes: #53337, #57174, #57712
related: #45930

pull_requests.body:
closes: #73803

Stacked on #72862 — that PR's commit is included in this branch's diff; only the second commit belongs to this change.

## Why

#72862 scopes `GET /ui/next_run_assets/{dag_id}` so `events` carries only the assets the caller may read, while `asset_expression` keeps a hidden slot for each unreadable one (#72864). `AssetSchedule.tsx` still derives both the total and its layout from `events`, so the Dag renders differently depending on who is looking at it.

For a Dag scheduled on assets A, B and C, a caller who may read only A sees:

- "0 of 1" instead of "0 of 3" — `scheduledTotal` is `nextRunEvents.length`.
- The single-asset layout instead of the popover, from the `nextRunEvents.length === 1` branch.
- No asset schedule at all if none are readable — the `!nextRunEvents.length` branch falls back to `timetableSummary`, hiding that the Dag is asset triggered.

The popover contents are already correct: `AssetExpression` renders the hidden slots.

## What

- `NextRunAssetsResponse` gains `scheduling_asset_count`: how many assets the Dag is scheduled on, counted before the readable filter narrows the query. It reveals nothing new — the redacted expression already carries one slot per asset.
- `AssetSchedule.tsx` uses it for `scheduledTotal` and for the two length-based branches. `scheduledCount` is unchanged: only readable, satisfied assets count as ready.

The count costs one extra query on an endpoint that renders once per Dag card, so `assert_queries_count` goes from 5 to 6. An alternative that avoids it — filtering unreadable rows in Python instead of SQL, taking the total from the unfiltered row count — would mean reworking #72862's approach; happy to switch if reviewers prefer that trade.

pull_requests.title: Regenerate provider requirement tables in breeze ci upgrade
pull_requests.body:
Raising dependency floors in `breeze ci upgrade` changes provider `pyproject.toml` files. The requirement tables rendered from them into provider `README.rst` and `docs/index.rst` are only refreshed by the `update-providers-build-files` and `sync-provider-readme` prek hooks. The upgrade job builds hook environments (`prek install-hooks`) but does not install the git hook, so the upgrade commit is made without them. Every upgrade PR that raised a provider floor therefore failed static checks until the tables were regenerated by hand, as on #73629.

The upgrade now runs both hooks right after the floor step, and `--no-upgrade-dependency-floors` skips them along with it, following the existing datamodel-regeneration step.

A Dag authored entirely in Java has no Python in the picture, but the native-Dag docs still taught its edge verbs as "Java's spelling of Python's `>>` and `<<`" and described the feature as "with no Python stub file". That asks the reader to know a language the feature does not involve.

```java
cleaned.after(loaded, transformed); // cleanup waits for load and transform
```

pull_requests.title: Read a mapped upstream's XCom sequence in chunks instead of one item per request
pull_requests.body:
> **Review only this change:** [the PR's own commit](https://github.com/apache/airflow/pull/73790/commits/198ee878edea0590ccb7d842e7020e184c33da04) · [diff against #62922's branch](https://github.com/dabla/airflow/compare/feature/dynamic-task-iteration...feature/xcom-sequence-chunked-reads). Everything else in this PR's commit list and file list is #62922, which this PR is stacked on.

Stacked on #62922 (Task Iteration): only the last commit, 198ee878ed, belongs to this PR. It will be rebased once #62922 merges.

related: #62922

## What

`LazyXComSequence`, the value a mapped upstream's `XComArg` resolves to, fetched one item per `GetXComSequenceItem` request. Iterating it, or an iterated task reading it by index (see #62922, where `.iterate()` resolves its input by index), cost one supervisor round trip to the API server per item, which is the dominant cost for large inputs.

Reads now come in chunks:

- An index outside the slice held fetches `chunk_size` items starting there with one `GetXComSequenceSlice` request, the message the slice path already used, and the consecutive reads that follow are served from it. Sequential access costs one request per chunk instead of one per item, on both the sync path (`__getitem__`/`__iter__` through `send`) and the async one (`aget`/`__aiter__` through `asend`), and at most one chunk is held in memory. A jump backwards fetches again from there.
- A negative index no longer needs its own per-item request: it is mapped from the end through the cached length, so one `GetXComCount` at most.
- The client no longer sends `GetXComSequenceItem` at all. The request handler and the API endpoint keep serving it, so nothing else changes.

The sync and async paths share the request builder and the response parser, so they cannot drift.

## Why

For a 17,000-item mapped upstream consumed by `.iterate()`, this is about 530 requests instead of 17,000. It is the "XCom slice optimisation" left out of #62922 on purpose, so that PR stays a pure simplification with unchanged behaviour.

## Chunk size

A new option, `[core] xcom_sequence_chunk_size`, default 32, described in `config.yml` next to `max_map_length` and mentioned in the iteration docs. It bounds memory at that many values of whatever size the XComs are, and larger values mean fewer round trips. `LazyXComSequence` reads it as its default and also accepts an explicit `chunk_size`.

## Tests

`test_lazy_sequence.py` now asserts slice requests, with the chunk size taken from the config option and given explicitly: one per chunk while iterating, none for a read within the held chunk, a new request on a jump backwards, and negative indices through the cached count on both paths. The mapped-operator fake supervisor honours slice bounds, which it previously ignored.

pull_requests.title: Refuse nested secret ids looked up with no team in multi-team mode
pull_requests.body:
In multi-team mode with team-scoped paths, the Vault and Akeyless secrets backends build a team's secret names under the same base path that a lookup with no team resolves in. A connection or variable id containing the path separator, looked up with no team, could therefore name a team's secret: `team1/db_password` resolved `{base_path}/team1/db_password`.

Such ids are now refused for a caller with no team, the same way both backends already refuse them for a caller with a team:

- **Vault** — refused when the id's path part (below the mount point) contains `/`, in multi-team mode with `use_team_secrets_path` enabled.
- **Akeyless** — refused under the same conditions unless `global_secrets_path` is set, which gives secrets used outside any team a namespace of their own; nested ids keep working there.

The Amazon, Azure and Yandex backends already refuse ids containing their team separator for every caller, so they need no change. Outside multi-team mode, or with `use_team_secrets_path=False`, nothing changes. Both provider changelogs carry a note, since nested ids looked up with no team stop resolving in the affected configuration.

pull_requests.title: Always clear the session cookie on logout
pull_requests.body:
When the auth manager supplies an external logout URL (FAB, Keycloak), `/auth/logout` revoked the token and redirected without deleting the `_token` cookie, so the revocation was the only thing ending the local session. `revoke_token` also caught every failure — including a failure to record the revocation — and logged it as a warning, so a revocation that did not happen looked the same as one that did.

- The `_token` cookie is now deleted on every logout path, including the redirect to an external logout URL. Neither the FAB nor the Keycloak logout route reads it (Keycloak uses the separate ID-token cookie).
- `revoke_token` separates a token that does not validate (already unusable, logged as a warning, as before) from a valid token whose revocation cannot be recorded, which stays usable until it expires and is now logged as an error.

The new route tests stub the refresh middleware so that only the logout route can clear the cookie.

pull_requests.title: Fix Python task startup with large integers in Dag run conf
pull_requests.body:
Python tasks fail before their task body runs when Dag run conf contains an integer such as `18446744073709551616`. The Execution API preserves the value, but encoding the supervisor's startup message raises `OverflowError` because it exceeds MessagePack's native integer range.

Preserve these values across Python subprocess communication using a MessagePack extension with a signed binary payload. Both directions restore the original Python `int`, including nested values. Conversion runs only after an encoding overflow, preserving the ordinary encoding path.

External language-SDK subprocesses retain their existing behavior, whether or not they specify a schema version: unsupported integers raise before any socket write. This change does not add large-integer support to external runtimes or dictionary keys.

Validation in Breeze with Python 3.10 and SQLite:

- Reproduced positive and negative overflow before the fix in real Python task startup and DB/Execution API tests.
- Communication, supervisor, subprocess coordinator, and schema integration tests: 425 passed, 1 platform-specific skip.
- DB/Execution API regression tests: 5 passed.
- External-runtime guard tests cover specified and unspecified schema versions and verify no socket write; they use the actual sender class with mock sockets.
- Ruff, Task SDK and core mypy, and applicable static checks passed. No live Celery/Kubernetes deployment was tested.

Broader validation: the API, Core, CLI, Other, and Serialization groups passed. pull_requests.title: Fix provider.yaml doc URL check with several suspended providers
pull_requests.body:
Continues #73204.

## Summary

Both suspended-provider filters in the `provider.yaml` check are nested-`for` comprehensions, so they keep an entry when **any** suspended provider fails to match it rather than when none do. Suspend two providers at once and each one's doc URLs survive, because the other suspended provider is absent from them — the check then reports them as missing from `provider.yaml` and fails on docs it was meant to ignore.

The error filter has the same shape, and additionally repeats every unrelated error once per suspended provider.

The cross product is accidentally correct for a single suspended provider, the only configuration the check has ever run with. With none suspended it emptied the set instead — what the two guards were covering for.

## Change

- Match every suspended provider against an entry rather than any one of them.
- Move both filters to `scripts/in_container/provider_suspension.py` so they can be tested.
- Cover zero, one and several suspended providers in the tests.

The filters moved because the check script refuses to be imported as a module; behaviour for a single suspended provider is unchanged.

## Compatibility

Matching stays substring-based: suspending `apache-airflow-providers-git` would also strip the `apache-airflow-providers-github` docs, as it does today. Narrowing it to the `/docs/<package-name>/` prefix is a separate change.

pull_requests.title: preserve last_finish_time in callback-only DagFileProcessorManager processing
pull_requests.body:
Fixes #73432 — the dag processor can get stuck in an infinite loop after a Dag-level callback runs.

Here's what happens: when a Dag file gets processed in "callback-only" mode (meaning it was triggered by a Dag callback, not a regular scan), `process_parse_results` creates a new `DagFileStat` with `last_finish_time=None`. That stat overwrites the existing one in `_file_stats`, so on the next scan the file looks like it's never been parsed. The scheduler re-queues it, processes it again, creates another stat with `last_finish_time=None`, and the cycle repeats forever.

The fix is to preserve the existing `last_finish_time` when doing callback-only processing. I added a `last_finish_time` parameter to `process_parse_results` — when it's passed (from the existing stat), the `is_callback_only` branch uses it instead of the current `finish_time`. I updated both call sites:

- `handle_parsing_result`: passes `self._file_stats[file].last_finish_time` — this is the main fix for the reported issue
- `process_unparsed_files`: passes `db_stat.last_finish_time` to `DagFileStat.from_db` — this handles the case where a file is already in the DB

I couldn't run the full airflow test suite here (the test environment needs a database and a bunch of infra), but I did validate the Python syntax with `py_compile` and the logic is pretty straightforward — it's just passing a timestamp through instead of dropping it.

pull_requests.title: Remove unused [scheduler] task_instance_heartbeat_sec option
pull_requests.body:
`[scheduler] task_instance_heartbeat_sec` has no effect in Airflow 3. Every task runs under the task supervisor, which takes its heartbeat interval from `[workers] min_heartbeat_interval`. Nothing reads `task_instance_heartbeat_sec`. The configuration reference still describes it as "The frequency (in seconds) at which the LocalTaskJob should send heartbeat signals to the scheduler". The "Reproducing task instance heartbeat timeouts locally" how-to sets it to slow heartbeats down.

The option is removed from `config.yml`. The how-to now sets `AIRFLOW__WORKERS__MIN_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL` instead. `airflow config lint` and `airflowctl config lint` report the option as removed and point at `min_heartbeat_interval`. Both commands reported the Airflow 2 name `local_task_job_heartbeat_sec` as renamed to `task_instance_heartbeat_sec`. They now report it as removed too. `airflow config update --fix --all-recommendations` rewrote the Airflow 2 name as `task_instance_heartbeat_sec`. It now removes both names.

The template default has to go with the lint rule. While `config.yml` defines the option, `conf.has_option` is true on every install. The removal rule would then flag every install.

The new parametrized lint tests in `airflow-core` and `airflow-ctl` cover both names. Their assertions fail without the source change and pass with it.

pull_requests.title: Allow explicit runs on a paused Dag without resuming its schedule
pull_requests.body: A paused Dag never starts the runs you trigger or backfill, so the only way to run them today is to unpause the Dag, which also resumes its schedule. That doesn't work for Dags that only reprocess historical data on demand: the scheduled runs fail or waste resources. An earlier attempt (#60818) let runs execute on a paused Dag and was closed, because a paused Dag should never run. This PR builds on the new `draining` state (#72407) instead. Draining already means "create no scheduled runs, finish the existing ones, then pause". Manual runs, backfills and asset materializations can now start that drain themselves. The run executes, the scheduler creates nothing new, and the Dag lands back on paused once its runs finish. The paused state keeps its meaning, and no new scheduling state is added. closes: #60768 ### What changes for users - **REST API**: `POST /dags/{dag_id}/dagRuns`, `POST /backfills` and `POST /assets/{asset_id}/materialize` accept `drain_dag` (default `false`). The Dag starts draining in the same transaction that creates the run (for a backfill, its runs), so a rejected or failed request leaves the Dag untouched. - **Permissions**: because draining changes the Dag's scheduling state, `drain_dag` also requires the permission `PATCH /dags/{dag_id}` needs to pause the Dag (`PUT` on the Dag), on top of the permission to create the run. - **UI**: on a paused Dag, the trigger, backfill and materialize forms replace the "Unpause on trigger" checkbox with a collapsible "Dag is paused" section. It offers three choices: *Unpause on trigger* (default, same as today), *Run without resuming the schedule* (drains), or *Leave paused*. The collapsed header shows the current choice. The forms fetch the Dag's paused state when they open, rather than using a value cached for up to five minutes, which could drain a Dag that was unpaused elsewhere in the meantime. When draining is chosen and the Dag already has unfinished runs, a warning says they will run too; runs of a paused backfill are not counted, since they do not start. - **airflowctl**: `dags trigger` and `backfill create` get `--drain-dag` through the regenerated datamodels. - **Docs**: the drain section in `core-concepts/dags.rst` and the backfill UI steps are updated, and the drain release note (`72407.significant.rst`) gains a paragraph, since both ship in 3.4.0. ### Behaviour worth reviewing - Draining lets **every** unfinished run proceed. On a paused Dag, runs that were already sitting in the queue start as well. Starting only the new run would need a per-run exemption from the paused check, which is the approach #60818 was closed for. The UI warns about this instead. - On an active Dag, `drain_dag` works like draining from the pause toggle: the schedule stops now and the Dag ends paused. - `DagModel.start_drain` locks the Dag row before the run is inserted. Otherwise the drain finalizer could pause an already-draining Dag at the same moment, leaving the new run stuck in the queue. Taking the lock before the insert also avoids upgrading the foreign-key lock the insert takes on MySQL. A backfill commits its row first, so it takes the lock afterwards, in the transaction that creates its runs: the drain then commits or rolls back with them, and the Dag row stays locked while they are created. ### Screenshots Taken on `example_bash_operator` in Breeze. | Trigger form on a paused Dag | Section expanded | |---|---| | | | | Draining with unfinished runs present | Backfill form | |---|---| | | | **Dag page after triggering with "Run without resuming the schedule"** --- ##### Was generative AI tooling used to co-author this PR? - [X] Yes — Claude Code (Opus 5.5) Generated-by: Claude Code (Opus 5.5) following [the guidelines](https://github.com/apache/airflow/blob/main/contributing-docs/05_pull_requests.rst#gen-ai-assisted-contributions)

pull_requests.title: Fix Snowflake SQL API wait_for_query timing out on finished queries
pull_requests.body:
`SnowflakeSqlApiHook.wait_for_query` checked the elapsed time before it looked at the status it had just fetched. If the status call itself returned after the timeout, the method raised `TimeoutError` even when that status showed the query had already finished (`success` or `error`).

This is easy to hit in practice. Each status call goes through `_make_api_call_with_retries`, which retries 429/503/504 and connection errors with exponential backoff, so one call can take several seconds. The only caller in the provider, the OpenLineage helper `_run_single_query_with_api_hook`, uses `timeout=3`. A slow but successful status check therefore surfaced as a timeout, and the query-history details for lineage were dropped.

Changes:

- the status is checked first; `TimeoutError` is raised only while the query is still `running`
- elapsed time uses `time.monotonic()` instead of `time.time()`, so wall-clock adjustments (NTP sync, DST) cannot cut the wait short or stretch it

Tests:

- new `test_wait_for_query_returns_finished_status_after_timeout_elapsed` (parametrized for `success` and `error`): a single status call that takes longer than the timeout returns the finished status instead of raising. It fails with the previous check order.
- `test_wait_for_query_timeout_error` now drives a fake monotonic clock, because `time_machine` does not move `time.monotonic()`. It still asserts the same number of polls and sleeps before `TimeoutError`.

Checks run locally:
- `uv run --project providers/snowflake pytest tests/unit/snowflake/hooks/test_snowflake_sql_api.py`: 91 passed
- `uv run --project providers/snowflake pytest tests/unit/snowflake/utils/test_openlineage.py`: 48 passed

This PR fixes the flaky test test_trigger_log: the loop now breaks as soon as both status lines arrive, and the upper bound is raised to 300 attempts (30 seconds) so a slow CI runner has enough headroom.

`test_trigger_log` gave the forked trigger runner a fixed budget of thirty `_service_subprocess(0.1)` calls before asserting on the "triggers currently running" / "watchers currently running" log lines. `_service_subprocess` returns as soon as any I/O arrives, so on a loaded CI runner that budget can be spent before the runner process has reached its status log. pull_requests.title: [SPARK-59713][SQL][TEST][4.x] Add a large-group case to `AsOfJoinBenchmark`
pull_requests.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

This PR adds a third shape to `AsOfJoinBenchmark`: 10K x 10K rows over **10** equi-key groups,
between the existing `groups=100` and no-equi-key cases. `asOfJoinBenchmark` already takes
`numGroups`, so this is purely a new invocation.

### Why are the changes needed?

`SortMergeAsOfJoinScanner` buffers the right-side rows of an equi-key group and rescans that
buffer once per left row, so the scan cost per left row grows with the group size. Neither
existing case covers that: `groups=100` buffers only ~100 right rows per group, where the scan is
swamped by the shuffle and the sort, and the no-equi-key case takes a different planning path
(`AllTuples` distribution, `bufferAllRight` instead of `bufferRightGroup`).

`groups=10` buffers ~1000 right rows per group on the ordinary equi-key path, making changes to
the scan measurable.

No. This is a test-only change to a benchmark class.

pull_requests.title: [SPARK-59827][CORE] Re-register a waiting task in ExecutionMemoryPool.acquireMemory after its entry is removed
pull_requests.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

`ExecutionMemoryPool.acquireMemory` registered the task's `memoryForTask` entry once, before its wait loop, and read it on every pass with `memoryForTask(taskAttemptId)`. `releaseMemory` removes the entry when the task's balance reaches zero and calls `notifyAll`. A caller parked in `lock.wait()` that woke after that removal threw `java.util.NoSuchElementException: key not found: <taskAttemptId>` instead of continuing to wait or being granted memory.

This PR moves the registration check to the top of each loop pass. A task whose entry was removed while it waited is re-registered at zero, and the existing `notifyAll` on registration wakes the other waiters so they recount the active tasks. The first pass behaves exactly as before.

The entry can be removed under a waiting caller because `TaskMemoryManager.releaseExecutionMemory` does not take the `TaskMemoryManager` monitor that `acquireExecutionMemory` holds while it waits. Any consumer of the same task that releases through it (`MemoryConsumer.freeMemory`, or a caller on another thread) can bring the balance to zero while another acquire of that task is parked below its share. Synchronizing the release on the `TaskMemoryManager` instead would deadlock with the parked acquirer, and keeping zero-balance entries in the pool would inflate the active task count after tasks end, so the loop is the right place for the fix.

One related edge case changes shape: if `releaseAllMemoryForTask` runs while a thread of that task is still parked in `acquireMemory`, the waiter previously threw the same exception; now it re-registers the task and can be granted memory, the same as a thread of that task that calls `acquireMemory` after cleanup already could.

### Why are the changes needed?

The exception is not a memory error, so callers such as `UnsafeExternalSorter` do not treat it as a signal to spill; the task fails. Seen in Apache DataFusion Comet, whose native memory consumer parks in this loop while other consumers of the same task release (apache/datafusion-comet#6224, apache/datafusion-comet#6304). Comet works around it by retrying the acquire.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

No.

### How was this patch tested?

New test in `MemoryManagerSuite` (runs for both the static and unified memory managers): with two tasks and no free memory, a task's acquire blocks below its 1 / 2N share, another thread of the same task frees its whole balance, and the blocked acquire must keep waiting and later be granted its 1 / N cap once the other task releases. The test fails before the fix (the future completes with the exception) and passes after. Ran `core/testOnly *MemoryManagerSuite *UnifiedMemoryManagerSuite *TestMemoryManagerSuite` and `core/scalastyle`.

### Was this patch authored or co-authored using generative AI tooling?

No

pull_requests.title: [SPARK-59829][SQL] Fix overflow in forward ASOF join by keeping the first match
pull_requests.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?
Forward ASOF joins (`t.k <= r.k` or `t.k < r.k`) in `SortMergeAsOfJoinExec` now keep the first right row that matches. Before, they reused the Nearest loop, which computes `right - left` for every candidate and keeps the smallest.

The right rows are sorted ascending, so the first match is always the closest one. This mirrors Backward, which keeps the last match. The operator now reads the direction (Backward, Forward, Nearest) from the as-of condition. Nearest, and any condition shape it does not recognize, keep the old distance loop.

### Why are the changes needed?
The subtraction overflows when values are far apart, even though the answer never needs it:

```sql
SET spark.sql.join.asofJoin.enabled=true;
SELECT r.tag
FROM VALUES (-100) AS t(k)
ASOF JOIN VALUES (-50, 'near'), (2147483647, 'far') AS r(k, tag)
  MATCH_CONDITION (t.k <= r.k);
```

- ANSI on: fails with `ARITHMETIC_OVERFLOW`.
- ANSI off: `2147483647 - (-100)` wraps to a negative number, so it returns `far`.
- Expected, and the result after this PR: `near`.

The same bug hits BIGINT, DECIMAL(38, 0), and both interval types, as an error or a wrong result.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?
No.

### How was this patch tested?
New tests in `AsOfJoinSortMergeSQLSuite`:
- One overflow test per type (INT, BIGINT, DECIMAL(38, 0), INTERVAL YEAR TO MONTH, INTERVAL DAY TO SECOND). Each runs `<=` and `<`, with ANSI on and off, and expects `near`.
- A forward test where the closest row fails an extra `ON` filter, so the join must skip it and return the next row.

pull_requests.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

This PR aims to implement `skipFixedLenByteArray` in `VectorizedDeltaByteArrayReader` by delegating to `skipBinary`, because `DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY` encodes `FIXED_LEN_BYTE_ARRAY` values in the same way as `BYTE_ARRAY` values.

### Why are the changes needed?

The Parquet v2 writer encodes `FIXED_LEN_BYTE_ARRAY` columns such as `DECIMAL(38, 18)` with `DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY` when dictionary encoding is disabled. When Parquet column index filtering skips rows of such a column, the vectorized reader fails because `VectorizedDeltaByteArrayReader` does not implement `skipFixedLenByteArray`.

```scala
spark.range(0, 2000).selectExpr("id as _1", "cast(id as decimal(38, 18)) as _2")
  .coalesce(1)
  .write
  .option("parquet.writer.version", "PARQUET_2_0")
  .option("parquet.enable.dictionary", "false")
  .option("parquet.page.size", "2048")
  .option("parquet.page.row.count.limit", "500")
  .parquet("t")
spark.read.parquet("t").filter("_1 >= 500 and _1 < 1000").collect()
```


No, this fixes a bug that has existed since Apache Spark [v3.3.0](https://github.com/apache/spark/releases/tag/v3.3.0) (2022-06-09) but it didn't work before.

pull_requests.title: [SPARK-59663][CONNECT][SDP] Keep pipeline flow dependencies when withColumns and withColumnsRenamed eagerly analyze
pull_requests.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

Spark Connect's `withColumns` and `withColumnsRenamed` try eager analysis first and fall back to a lazily resolved plan (`UnresolvedStarWithColumns` / `UnresolvedStarWithColumnsRenames`) when it fails (SPARK-53505).

This PR plans Declarative Pipelines flow relations without that eager analysis:

- `SparkConnectPlanner.transformRelationWithoutEagerAnalysis` transforms a relation with the eager analysis of `withColumns` / `withColumnsRenamed` disabled, and `handlePipelineCommand` hands it to `PipelinesHandler` instead of `transformRelation`. `PipelinesHandler` uses it only in `defineFlow`.
- Both call sites now go through a shared `tryEagerAnalysis` helper, which returns the lazy plan directly when eager analysis is disabled and otherwise behaves exactly as before.

Nothing changes outside pipelines, and no configuration is added.

### Why are the changes needed?

`FlowAnalysis` discovers a flow's dependencies by matching `UnresolvedRelation`s in the flow's plan. `PipelinesHandler.defineFlow` runs the flow relation through the planner at `DefineFlow` time:

- **First run (clean catalog):** the upstream table does not exist, eager analysis fails, the fallback keeps the `UnresolvedRelation`, and the dependency is recorded.
- **Every later run:** the upstream table now exists, eager analysis succeeds and consumes the `UnresolvedRelation` against the *stale catalog table*. `FlowAnalysis` records no dependency, and the downstream flow is scheduled concurrently with its own upstream.

Result from the JIRA repro: on the second run `b = spark.read.table("a").withColumn(...)` starts before `a` and ends up with **0 rows**, while the equivalent `select(...)` flow `c` is correct. The bug passes every first-run smoke test and only shows up on scheduled re-runs.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes, a bug fix. Pipeline flows that use `withColumn(s)` / `withColumnRenamed` / `withColumnsRenamed` on another pipeline dataset now keep their dependency on that dataset across runs, so they wait for it instead of reading a stale or empty table. Non-pipeline Spark Connect queries are unaffected.

### How was this patch tested?

Added `SPARK-59663: withColumns and withColumnsRenamed keep the dependency on an internal dataset that already exists in the catalog` to `PythonPipelineSuite`. It pre-creates `spark_catalog.default.src` (simulating a previous run), defines `src` plus a `withColumn` flow and a `withColumnRenamed` flow on it, and asserts each flow's inputs are `{src}`.

- Without the fix, the test fails for both flows (each verified separately): `Set() did not equal Set(spark_catalog.default.src)`.
- With the fix, `PythonPipelineSuite`, `SparkConnectPlannerSuite`, `SparkConnectProtoSuite` and `PipelinesHandlerSuite` pass (222 tests).

```
build/sbt 'connect/testOnly *PythonPipelineSuite *SparkConnectPlannerSuite *SparkConnectProtoSuite *PipelinesHandlerSuite'
```

Note: if user code explicitly analyzes a DataFrame *outside* the flow function (e.g. `df.columns`), the resulting plan can come from the session plan cache. That path already fails on a clean catalog, and the existing test `reading internal datasets outside query function that trigger eager analysis or execution will fail` covers it as unsupported, so it is left out of scope here.

pull_requests.title: [SPARK-59825][SQL][TESTS] Fix `HiveClientSuites` to work with sbt `testOnly` and `-z` filtering
pull_requests.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?
`HiveClientSuites` runs `HiveClientSuite` once per supported Hive metastore (HMS) version by exposing them through ScalaTest's `nestedSuites`. This pattern does not interoperate well with SBT's ScalaTest framework integration, and this PR fixes two resulting problems:

1. `testOnly ... -- -z "<keyword>"` reports "No tests were executed" because the ScalaTest SBT framework cannot propagate the test-name filter down to the nested suites (their `suiteId`s differ from the parent's).
2. During a full run, test names and version info for HMS versions other than the first are not displayed properly.

The fix works around a known ScalaTest limitation (https://github.com/scalatest/scalatest/issues/2375):

- `HiveClientSuites`
  - Override `testNames` to include the nested suites' test names so that the SBT framework's `-z` substring matching can see them.
  - Override `run` to handle both filtered (`-z`/`-t`) and full runs. The SBT ScalaTest framework always calls `run` with `testName == None` and encodes any selection as a `Selected` tag plus per-test `dynaTags` keyed by this suite's `suiteId`; because our `testNames` exposes the nested names, those selections land in this suite's`dynaTags`. The override runs our own tests separately (filtered against`super.testNames`), then re-keys the matching `dynaTags` to each nested suite's`suiteId` and runs it once. Own tests and nested-suite tests are dispatched separately so a full run never double-executes.
  - Factor the per-suite `SuiteStarting`/`SuiteCompleted`/`SuiteAborted` reporting into a private `runNestedSuiteWithEvents` helper (needed because each nested suite must receive its own re-keyed `Filter`, so `runNestedSuites` cannot be used directly).
  - Make `nestedSuites` a `lazy val` so the nested suites are not re-created on every call.
- `HiveVersionSuite`
  - Override `suiteId` to `s"${getClass.getName}($version)"` so each version's nested suite has a unique `suiteId` (required for the `dynaTags` redistribution above).
- `HiveClientSuite`
  - Move client construction/teardown from the `"create client"` test body into `beforeAll`/`afterAll`, so that running a single test via `-z` still initializes `client`/`versionSpark`. The `"create client"` test now asserts they were initialized in `beforeAll`.

Note on scope: the nested `HiveClientSuite` tests are order-dependent -- they share a single `client`/`versionSpark` and many tests rely on state (databases, tables, partitions, functions) created by earlier tests. Selecting a single order-dependent test with `-z` runs it in isolation and may fail because its prerequisites were filtered out; independent tests (e.g. `"create client"`) can be selected safely. This is a pre-existing property of these tests and is called out in a code comment; making them self-contained is left to a separate change. Only `HiveClientSuites` is converted here; the sibling `HiveClientUserNameSuites` / `HivePartitionFilteringSuites` use the same `nestedSuites` pattern and can be converted the same way in follow-ups.

### Why are the changes needed?
Developers cannot currently run a single Hive client test (or a subset) via SBT's `-z` filter -- the run silently executes nothing, which is easy to misread as "passed". This makes iterating on Hive client changes slow and error-prone. The full-run display issue also hides which HMS versions actually ran.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?
No. This only affects test-suite execution/reporting for `HiveClientSuites`.

### How was this patch tested?
Existing tests, plus manual verification against `master` and this branch (JDK 17, `build/sbt`):

- Reproduced the bug on `master`:

  ```
  build/sbt 'hive/testOnly org.apache.spark.sql.hive.client.HiveClientSuites \
    -- -z "should pick right user name as owner"'
  ```

  -> `Total number of tests run: 0` / `No tests were executed.`

- On this branch, the same command runs the selected test across all HMS versions:

  -> `Total number of tests run: 8` / `succeeded 8, failed 0` / `All tests passed.`

- Full run on this branch is unaffected:

  ```
  build/sbt 'hive/testOnly org.apache.spark.sql.hive.client.HiveClientSuites'
  ```

  -> `595 succeeded, 0 failed` and test names for all HMS versions (2.0 / 2.1 / 2.2 / 2.3 / 3.0 / 3.1 / 4.0 / 4.1) are displayed (problem 2 fixed), with no double execution.

- After the review-driven cleanup (removing the unreachable `runTest` override, extracting `runNestedSuiteWithEvents`, switching to `NonFatal`), re-verified that behavior is unchanged: `hive/Test/compile` succeeds, `-z` selection still runs the selected test across all 8 HMS versions (8 passed, one `beforeAll` per version), the full run is still `595 succeeded, 0 failed` with all versions listed, and `hive/scalastyle` reports 0 errors.

Note: order-dependent tests in `HiveClientSuite` (e.g. `getTablesByName when multiple tables`, which relies on the earlier `createTable` test) will fail if selected alone with `-z`. That is a pre-existing property of these tests, out of scope here, and is tracked separately.

pull_requests.title: [SPARK-59821][CORE] Make Maven utility tests safe for concurrent runs
pull_requests.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

This follow-up to #58874 makes the Maven test utilities safe when the same suite runs concurrently.

- Compile generated Java classes in an invocation-specific temporary directory instead of the process working directory.
- Give each test JVM its own stable fake local Maven repository.
- Add a regression test that compiles the same class name concurrently into separate destinations.

### Why are the changes needed?

`SparkTestUtils.createCompiledClass` currently asks javac to emit a fixed class name, such as `MyLib.class`, in the process working directory before moving it to the requested destination. `MavenUtils.m2Path` also uses the fixed relative path `dummy/.m2/repository` during tests.

When a test target is repeated concurrently, the JVMs can move or delete files needed by another JVM. This causes failures such as:

```
java.nio.file.NoSuchFileException:
  MyLib.class -> dummy/.m2/repository/.../MyLib.class
```

Using isolated temporary paths removes this cross-JVM interference without changing production Maven resolution.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

No.

### How was this patch tested?

Added a `SparkTestUtilsSuite` regression test that starts eight concurrent compilations of the same class name and verifies every output exists.

`git diff --check` passes.

The following focused command was attempted locally:

```
/usr/bin/sbt \
  "common-utils/testOnly org.apache.spark.util.SparkTestUtilsSuite" \
  "common-utils/testOnly org.apache.spark.util.MavenUtilsSuite"
```

The suites could not start because the local environment could not resolve Maven Central or the SBT plugin repositories (`UnknownHostException`). GitHub Actions will provide the executable test result.

pull_requests.title: [SPARK-59524][CORE] Enforce the array-key / HashPartitioner guard in subtractByKey and the Java fakeClassTag key path
pull_requests.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?
In [SPARK-58758](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-58758) (PR #58758), array keys were prohibited in `HashPartitioner` and operations relying on array hashing (`partitionBy`, `combineByKeyWithClassTag`, `aggregateByKey`, `foldByKey`, `cogroup`). However, two gaps remained:
1. **`subtractByKey`**: `PairRDDFunctions.subtractByKey` creates a `SubtractedRDD` directly and defaults to `HashPartitioner`, but never called `failOnHashPartitionerWithArrayKey(p)`. Because `SubtractedRDD` matches array keys by reference identity, `arrPairs.subtractByKey(arrPairs)` silently returned every element instead of subtracting matching keys. This PR adds `failOnHashPartitionerWithArrayKey(p)` in `subtractByKey`.
2. **Java API `fakeClassTag`**: In the Java API, `JavaSparkContext.parallelizePairs` and `JavaPairRDD.fromJavaRDD` defaulted to `fakeClassTag` (`ClassTag.AnyRef`, whose runtime class is `Object`). Consequently, `keyClass.isArray` evaluated to `false`, and `byte[]` keys bypassed the array-key guard in `JavaPairRDD.partitionBy`, `join`, `cogroup`, and `subtractByKey`.
   - In `JavaSparkContext.parallelizePairs`, the key/value `ClassTag`s are now dynamically resolved from non-null elements in the driver-side in-memory collection.
   - In `JavaPairRDD`, overloaded `fromJavaRDD` methods accepting `keyClass: Class[K]` / `valueClass: Class[V]` are added with `@Since("4.4.0")` to allow Java callers to explicitly provide key type information across JVM generic type erasure.

### Why are the changes needed?
- Array hashing in Java produces reference-based hash codes rather than content-based hash codes, causing incorrect partitioning, grouping, and subtraction.
- Without these fixes, array keys in `subtractByKey` silently produce incorrect results, and Java pair RDDs with array keys completely evade the safety guard introduced in SPARK-58758.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?
Yes. Calling `subtractByKey` or Java pair operations (`partitionBy`, `join`, `cogroup`, `subtractByKey`) on an RDD with array keys and a `HashPartitioner` will now fail fast with `SparkException: [UNSUPPORTED_ARRAY_KEY.HASH_PARTITIONER]` rather than silently returning incorrect results.

### How was this patch tested?
- Added `subtractByKey` test cases in `core/src/test/scala/org/apache/spark/PartitioningSuite.scala`.
- Added `testArrayKeyUnderHashPartitionerFails` in `core/src/test/java/test/org/apache/spark/JavaAPISuite.java`.
- Ran:
  - `build/sbt "core/testOnly org.apache.spark.PartitioningSuite"`
  - `build/sbt "core/testOnly test.org.apache.spark.JavaAPISuite"`
  - `build/sbt core/scalastyle`

No.

pull_requests.title: [SPARK-59818][SQL] Handle a NULL sketch state in approx_top_k_estimate and approx_top_k_combine
pull_requests.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

Fixes [SPARK-59818](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-59818) — makes `approx_top_k_estimate` and `approx_top_k_combine` handle a NULL sketch state instead of throwing `NullPointerException`. Two related gaps are addressed:

**`approx_top_k_estimate` dereferenced the state unconditionally.** `ApproxTopKEstimate` overrides `BinaryExpression.eval` directly rather than implementing `nullSafeEval`, so the inherited null handling is bypassed, and `eval` calls `stateEval.asInstanceOf[InternalRow].getBinary(0)` with no null check. It also declared `override def nullable: Boolean = false` even though the result is NULL whenever the state is, so the reported output schema was wrong and the optimizer reasoned incorrectly about the expression.

**`approx_top_k_combine` had the same unguarded dereference in `update`.** `ApproxTopKCombine.update` calls `inputState.getBinary(0)` directly, so a NULL sketch fails on the executors and aborts the running job, rather than being ignored the way aggregates normally ignore NULL inputs.

Analysis does not prevent either case: `checkStateFieldAndType` validates only the *schema* of the state struct, not its nullness, so a correctly-typed nullable struct column passes the analyzer and then fails at optimization or execution time. A NULL sketch arises naturally from an outer join, a `UNION` with a missing side, or a partially-populated column.

Both are surfaced and locked down by new tests.

**Brief change log**

- `sql/catalyst/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/sql/catalyst/expressions/ApproxTopKExpressions.scala`: `ApproxTopKEstimate.eval` returns `null` when the state evaluates to `null`, and `nullable` is now `state.nullable` instead of a hardcoded `false`, so the reported schema matches the values actually produced.
- `sql/catalyst/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/sql/catalyst/expressions/aggregate/ApproxTopKAggregates.scala`: `ApproxTopKCombine.update` returns the buffer untouched for a NULL sketch, so combine ignores NULL inputs like any other aggregate.
- `sql/core/src/test/scala/org/apache/spark/sql/ApproxTopKSuite.scala`: added four tests covering the foldable NULL state, the non-foldable NULL state, the reported nullability, and combine skipping NULL sketches.

### Why are the changes needed?

Both paths fail on a valid query.

`approx_top_k_estimate` raises the NPE inside `ConstantFolding`, which reports it to the user as an internal error:

```sql
SELECT approx_top_k_estimate(s, 5) FROM (
  SELECT CAST(NULL AS STRUCT<sketch: BINARY, maxItemsTracked: INT,
    itemDataType: INT, itemDataTypeDDL: STRING>) AS s
);
```

```
[INTERNAL_ERROR] The Spark SQL phase optimization failed with an internal error.
You hit a bug in Spark or the Spark plugins you use. SQLSTATE: XX000

Caused by: java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke
  "org.apache.spark.sql.catalyst.InternalRow.getBinary(int)" because "stateEval" is null
  at ApproxTopKEstimate.eval(ApproxTopKExpressions.scala:113)
  at org.apache.spark.sql.catalyst.optimizer.ConstantFolding$.tryFold(expressions.scala:65)
```

`approx_top_k_combine` fails on the executors and aborts the job:

```sql
SELECT approx_top_k_estimate(approx_top_k_combine(s), 5) FROM (
  SELECT CAST(NULL AS STRUCT<sketch: BINARY, maxItemsTracked: INT,
    itemDataType: INT, itemDataTypeDDL: STRING>) AS s
);
```

```
org.apache.spark.SparkException: Job aborted due to stage failure:
  Task 0 in stage 0.0 failed 1 times ...
Caused by: java.lang.NullPointerException
  at ApproxTopKCombine.update(ApproxTopKAggregates.scala:908)
  at TypedImperativeAggregate.update(interfaces.scala:583)
```

The new behaviour follows ordinary SQL semantics for a nullable input column: `approx_top_k_estimate(NULL, k)` returns NULL, and `approx_top_k_combine` skips NULL sketches.

This is distinct from the existing `APPROX_TOP_K_NULL_ARG` error, which is raised for NULL *foldable configuration* arguments (`k`, `maxItemsTracked`). That check, `ApproxTopK.checkExpressionNotNull`, calls `expr.eval()` with no input row, so it applies only to literals and is not applicable to a per-row data column.

It is also distinct from earlier NULL-related work on these functions. SPARK-53960 added handling for NULLs *within* the accumulated data (counting them as items) and did not touch the NULL-state path or the `nullable` declaration; SPARK-58095 concerns *empty* input (zero rows) in combine's `eval`/`serialize`, which is a different code path and trigger.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes, in three ways, all aligning the functions with ordinary SQL null semantics:

1. `approx_top_k_estimate` on a NULL sketch state returns NULL instead of failing the query with `[INTERNAL_ERROR]`.
2. `approx_top_k_combine` skips NULL sketches instead of aborting the job with a `NullPointerException`.
3. `approx_top_k_estimate` now reports itself as nullable when its state argument is nullable. Previously it always reported `nullable = false`, which was incorrect for a nullable state. The reported schema is unchanged for a non-nullable state, which is the common case — the `sql-expression-schema.md` golden file is unaffected, as its example applies the function to an aggregate result.

These are changes compared to released versions: `approx_top_k` is annotated `since = "4.1.0"`.

### How was this patch tested?

Four new tests in `ApproxTopKSuite`, covering both functions:

- `SPARK-59818: estimate of a foldable NULL state returns NULL`
- `SPARK-59818: estimate of a non-foldable NULL state returns NULL`
- `SPARK-59818: estimate is nullable when its state is nullable`
- `SPARK-59818: combine skips NULL sketches`

pull_requests.title: [SPARK-59819][CORE] Fix `Resubmitted` task end accounting in `AppStatusListener`
pull_requests.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

This PR aims to fix two `Resubmitted` accounting bugs in `AppStatusListener.onTaskEnd`.

When an executor is lost, `TaskSetManager.executorLost` posts `SparkListenerTaskEnd` with `Resubmitted` reason for the already-successful shuffle map tasks of that executor (without external shuffle service or on decommission) if the task set is not zombie. This event reuses the finished `TaskInfo` of the successful attempt and has no matching `SparkListenerTaskStart`. Since SPARK-41187 (apache/spark#38702), `onTaskEnd` uses `activeDelta = 0` for `Resubmitted`, but the following places still handle it like a normal task end.

1. The speculation summary decrements `numActiveTasks` unconditionally. This PR uses `activeDelta` like the other active task counters.
2. `ExecutorStageSummary.taskTime` and `ExecutorSummary.totalDuration` add `event.taskInfo.duration` again although the duration of the successful attempt was already counted. This PR skips them for `Resubmitted` like the executor-level task metrics, which are already skipped for `Resubmitted`.

### Why are the changes needed?

To show correct values.

- When a successful speculative task is resubmitted, `numActiveTasks` of the speculation summary becomes negative (e.g. `-1`), and nothing corrects it later because only `onTaskStart` and `onTaskEnd` update it. This value is stored in `SpeculationStageSummaryWrapper` and shown via the REST API `speculationSummary` field and the `Speculation Summary` table of the stage page.
- For every `Resubmitted` task end, the duration of the successful attempt is counted twice in `ExecutorStageSummary.taskTime` (`Task Time` of `Aggregated Metrics by Executor` table in the stage page). `ExecutorSummary.totalDuration` (`Task Time (GC Time)` in the executors page and `totalDuration_seconds_total` in the Prometheus metrics) is also counted twice if the `Resubmitted` task end arrives before `SparkListenerExecutorRemoved` of the lost executor. This is timing-dependent because `CoarseGrainedSchedulerBackend` posts `SparkListenerExecutorRemoved` right after `TaskSchedulerImpl.executorLost`, while the `Resubmitted` task end is posted asynchronously by the `DAGScheduler` event loop. Note that the old `ExecutorsListener` of Apache Spark 2.2 ignored `Resubmitted` task ends including the duration, but SPARK-20646 (apache/spark#19678) kept only the task metrics part when porting it to `AppStatusListener`.

These were found during the review of apache/spark#58968.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes, this fixes the incorrect values in the Spark UI, REST API, and Prometheus metrics. The negative `numActiveTasks` of the speculation summary exists since Apache Spark [v3.3.0](https://github.com/apache/spark/releases/tag/v3.3.0) (2022-06-09), and the double-counted task duration exists since Apache Spark [v2.3.0](https://github.com/apache/spark/releases/tag/v2.3.0) (2018-02-22).

### How was this patch tested?

Pass the CIs with the newly added test case. I also manually verified that the new test case fails without this fix.

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

This follow-up restores the three-way contract for `spark.sql.optimizer.nullAwareAntiJoinBroadcastThreshold`:

- A negative value allows the specialized null-aware anti join broadcast hash path without a size limit.
- Zero always disables that hash path.
- A positive value admits the path when either the dedicated threshold or the applicable automatic broadcast threshold allows it.

It updates the shared join-selection logic, configuration documentation, and optimizer and execution tests.

### Why are the changes needed?

SPARK-36082 established zero as the sentinel for disabling broadcast NAAJ. SPARK-59673 made the automatic broadcast threshold a floor, but unintentionally allowed that threshold to override zero. This restores the existing disable sentinel while preserving the automatic-threshold floor for positive dedicated thresholds.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes. On current master, setting `spark.sql.optimizer.nullAwareAntiJoinBroadcastThreshold` to zero once again disables the specialized NAAJ broadcast hash path even when an automatic broadcast threshold is positive. This corrects behavior introduced by the unreleased SPARK-59673 change.

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?
When `spark.ui.reverseProxy=true` is enabled in Standalone multi-cluster deployments:
1. `SparkContext` on the driver did not receive `UI_REVERSE_PROXY_URL`, causing driver UI links to drop `/proxy/<id>` prefixes. This PR propagates `UI_REVERSE_PROXY_URL` (or falls back to `spark.ui.proxyBase`) into system property `spark.ui.proxyBase`.

5. `SparkContext.stop()` was updated to restore `spark.ui.proxyBase` before `clearActiveContext()` to prevent race conditions with replacement contexts.

### Why are the changes needed?
Without these changes, multi-cluster reverse proxy deployments lose proxy prefixes when accessing driver UIs or terminating applications/drivers from Master UI, breaking navigation and reverse proxy routing.

No API changes. Fixes UI navigation links and redirect Location headers when `spark.ui.reverseProxy=true` is enabled.

pull_requests.title: [SPARK-59812][SQL] Validate value lengths and skip amounts in the vectorized PLAIN, DELTA_LENGTH_BYTE_ARRAY and DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY readers
pull_requests.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

Similar to SPARK-59352, this validates lengths read from the file in the vectorized PLAIN, DELTA_LENGTH_BYTE_ARRAY and DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY readers, mainly for their skip paths.

`VectorizedPlainValuesReader`:
- Add `readLength()`, which rejects a binary length that is negative or larger than the bytes left in the page, and use it in `readBinary`, `skipBinary` and `readGeoData`.
- Add `VectorizedReaderBase.skipFully(ByteBufferInputStream, long)`, which throws a `ParquetDecodingException` when the page has fewer bytes than requested, and use it in `skipBinary`, `skipBooleans` and all fixed-width skips (`skipIntegers`, `skipLongs`, `skipFloats`, `skipDoubles`, `skipBytes`, `skipShorts`, `skipFixedLenByteArray`). The fixed-width skips still do a single call per batch.

`VectorizedDeltaLengthByteArrayReader`:
- Validate all value lengths once in `initFromPage`: their count must not exceed the page's value count, each must be non-negative, and their sum must fit in the bytes left in the page. Values are consumed in order, so no later read or skip can run past the end of the page.
- Check that the rows consumed by `readBinary`, `readGeoData`, `skipBinary` and `getBytes` have a decoded length.
- Rewrite `skipBinary` to sum the lengths of the batch and skip them with a single `skipFully`, replacing the `remaining -= in.skip(remaining)` loop.
- Rename the package-private count getter to `getTotalValueCount()`, matching `VectorizedDeltaBinaryPackedReader`.

`VectorizedDeltaByteArrayReader`:
- Reject a page with more prefix lengths than values, or whose prefix length count differs from its suffix count.
- Get the suffix, which checks that the row was decoded, before reading the prefix length, so an undecoded row reports the row count instead of a misleading prefix length error.

### Why are the changes needed?

The skip paths are used when column-index filtering produces row ranges, and they did not validate what they read from the file, while the read paths mostly did. In Parquet 1.18.1, `SingleBufferInputStream.skip(n)` (what Spark gets for a data page) returns -1 at the end of the buffer, skips fewer bytes when the buffer is short, and moves the position backwards for a negative `n`. As a result, on a corrupt page:

- `VectorizedDeltaLengthByteArrayReader.skipBinary` with a length past the end of the page: `in.skip` returns -1, so `remaining` grows until the int overflows (about 2^31 iterations per value), then the read silently continues. A negative length is silently skipped.
- `VectorizedPlainValuesReader.skipBinary` with a negative length moves the stream position backwards, so the following values in the page are decoded from the wrong offset and the query returns wrong results without an error. For example, for a page `[4]"abcd"[-12]"zzzz"`, alternating read and skip returns `"abcd"` repeatedly.
- The fixed-width skips and `skipBinary` in the PLAIN reader silently skip fewer bytes than requested when the page is too short.
- `readGeoData` in both readers uses `in.readNBytes(len)`, which returns a short array instead of failing when a length runs past the end of the page.
- In the DELTA_LENGTH_BYTE_ARRAY and DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY readers, the number of decoded lengths was not checked against the page's value count: a larger count failed with an `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`, and rows past a smaller count silently read a zero length.
- On the read paths, a negative length was not rejected either. Slicing a negative length also moves the position backwards, or fails with an `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` instead of a `ParquetDecodingException`.

Note that `ByteBufferInputStream.skipFully` alone does not reject a negative `n` on `SingleBufferInputStream` (`skip(n)` returns `n`, so the `skipped < n` check passes), so negative lengths need an explicit check.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Only for corrupt Parquet files: reading a page with an invalid value length, an inconsistent length count, or too few bytes for the values being skipped now fails with a `ParquetDecodingException` instead of silently returning wrong values or spinning. Valid files are not affected.

### How was this patch tested?

New unit tests. Except for the DELTA_LENGTH_BYTE_ARRAY geo test, the negative tests in the first two suites run both on a single buffer and on the same page split across multiple buffers, since `SingleBufferInputStream` and `MultiBufferInputStream` handle short and negative lengths differently:
- `VectorizedPlainValuesReaderSuite` (new): negative and oversized (up to `Int.MaxValue`) binary lengths on read and skip, the same on the geo paths, every fixed-width skip (and `skipBooleans`) past the end of the page, and skips within the page landing on the next value.
- `ParquetDeltaLengthByteArrayEncodingSuite`: negative and oversized (up to `Int.MaxValue`) value lengths, more value lengths than values, and rows without a decoded length on `readBinary`, `skipBinary`, `getBytes` and the geo paths.
- `ParquetDeltaByteArrayEncodingSuite`: more prefix lengths than values, prefix length and suffix counts that differ, and an undecoded row reporting the row count rather than a prefix length error.

All the new negative tests fail without this change. Existing suites also pass: `ParquetDeltaByteArrayEncodingSuite`, `ParquetEncodingSuite`, `ParquetVectorizedSuite`, `ParquetColumnIndexSuite`, `ParquetVectorUpdaterSuite` and `ParquetIOSuite`.

pull_requests.title: [SPARK-59251][SQL] Reject incompatible Parquet row reader conversions
pull_requests.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

This pull request supersedes and completes the work originally started in **#58496** by @Jiayi-Wang-db (addressing **#58495** / **[SPARK-59251](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-59251)**).

While #58496 proposed rejecting two specific conversions, this PR provides a comprehensive fix to make the Parquet row-based reader (`ParquetRowConverter`) consistently reject all incompatible primitive type conversions that the vectorized reader already rejects with `SchemaColumnConvertNotSupportedException`:

1. **Decimal Conversion Validation (`canReadAsDecimal`)**:
   Check the logical type annotation for `INT32` and `INT64` columns when converting to `DecimalType`. Conversions are accepted only when the logical annotation is `DecimalLogicalTypeAnnotation`, unannotated (`null`), or a signed integer (`IntLogicalTypeAnnotation` with `isSigned=true`). Semantic types such as `DATE`, `TIMESTAMP`, `TIME`, and unsigned integers (`UINT32`) are rejected.

2. **Guarded String Conversions**:
   Guard `case _: StringType` in `ParquetRowConverter` with `parquetType.isPrimitive && parquetType.asPrimitiveType().getPrimitiveTypeName == BINARY`. Other physical primitives (`FIXED_LEN_BYTE_ARRAY`, `INT96`, `INT32`, `INT64`, `BOOLEAN`, `FLOAT`, `DOUBLE`) now throw `SchemaColumnConvertNotSupportedException`. Complex non-primitive groups requested as string cleanly throw `QueryExecutionErrors.cannotCreateParquetConverterForDataTypeError`.

3. **Column Path Error Parameter Alignment**:
   Thread `fieldPath: Seq[String]` through `ParquetRowConverter` and all nested converters (`ParquetArrayConverter`, `ElementConverter`, `ParquetMapConverter`, `KeyValueConverter`, `RepeatedPrimitiveConverter`, `RepeatedGroupConverter`) so `columnPath` formats as `[c]` or `[parent, child]`, matching `Arrays.toString(descriptor.getPath())` produced by the vectorized reader.

### Why are the changes needed?

Previously, the row-based reader silently accepted incompatible conversions or failed with internal decoding exceptions:
- `DATE` (`INT32`) was silently read as unscaled decimal values (e.g. date `2020-01-01` read as decimal `18262`).
- `FIXED_LEN_BYTE_ARRAY` and `INT96` raw bytes were silently decoded as corrupt UTF-8 strings.
- `INT32`/`INT64` to `STRING` failed with internal `ParquetDecodingException` rather than Spark's standard column type mismatch error.

Both Parquet readers should reject unsupported primitive conversions consistently with `FAILED_READ_FILE.PARQUET_COLUMN_DATA_TYPE_MISMATCH` instead of returning reader-dependent results or corrupt data.

Closes #58495.
Supersedes #58496.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes. When reading Parquet files with the row reader (e.g. with the vectorized reader disabled or falling back to the row reader), the following incompatible conversions now fail fast with `FAILED_READ_FILE.PARQUET_COLUMN_DATA_TYPE_MISMATCH` instead of returning corrupt data:
- `INT32` annotated as `DATE` -> `DecimalType`
- `INT64` annotated as `TIMESTAMP` / `TIME` -> `DecimalType`
- `INT32` annotated as `UINT32` -> `DecimalType`
- `FIXED_LEN_BYTE_ARRAY` -> `StringType`
- `INT96` -> `StringType`
- `INT32` / `INT64` / `BOOLEAN` / `FLOAT` / `DOUBLE` -> `StringType`

Valid conversions (e.g. `BINARY` -> `STRING`, unannotated `INT32`/`INT64` -> `DECIMAL`) remain unaffected.

### How was this patch tested?

- Added `ParquetIOSuite`: `SPARK-59251: Parquet readers reject incompatible primitive type conversions consistently` testing `INT32 DATE -> Decimal`, `FIXED_LEN_BYTE_ARRAY -> String`, `INT96 -> String`, and `INT64 Timestamp -> Decimal` across all Parquet readers.
- Updated `ParquetSchemaSuite`: unified `schema mismatch failure error message` for both vectorized and row readers to check `SchemaColumnConvertNotSupportedException` and parameter matches.
- Updated `ParquetTypeWideningSuite`: added `DateType -> DecimalType(10, 0)` to the unsupported conversions table.
- Verified all targeted test suites pass locally via SBT.
- Verified `sql/scalastyle` passes cleanly with 0 errors.

pull_requests.title: [SPARK-44517][SQL] Preserve nullability in batch deduplication
pull_requests.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

Preserve non-key attribute nullability in `ReplaceDeduplicateWithAggregate`: wrap the generated `First` aggregate with `KnownNotNull` only when its input attribute is non-nullable. Retain the generated-alias cache and leave nullable attributes and streaming deduplication unchanged.

This is safe specifically for this rewrite: the rule always produces a grouping aggregate, adding a literal grouping key when the deduplication key list is empty. Every output group therefore contains an input row. The general `First` expression is not changed.

Add optimizer, batch aggregation, and Data Source V2 write regressions, plus a SQL migration note.

### Why are the changes needed?

The rule currently replaces each non-key attribute with `first(attribute)`, whose result is nullable in general. This widens a non-nullable input column's schema during optimization. An otherwise-valid write to a Data Source V2 `NOT NULL` column then becomes unresolved and fails with `PLAN_VALIDATION_FAILED_RULE_IN_BATCH`.

For example, a non-nullable `value` in `spark.range(3).selectExpr("id", "id + 10 AS value").dropDuplicates("id")` becomes nullable in the optimized plan, and appending it to a table declared as `(id BIGINT NOT NULL, value BIGINT NOT NULL)` fails.

This follows the scoped approach discussed by Josh Rosen in [SPARK-44517](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-44517). Unlike the earlier, now-closed #42117 approach, it does not change `First.nullable` globally: global aggregation over empty input and `first(..., true)` over all-null input must remain nullable.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes. Batch `dropDuplicates` preserves non-key column nullability through optimization, allowing writes to compatible `NOT NULL` columns. Empty-input deduplication still returns no rows. The normal `first` aggregate retains its existing null behavior.

### How was this patch tested?

- Before the fix, the new optimizer regression failed; both codegen modes reproduced the schema change; the Data Source V2 append reproduced `PLAN_VALIDATION_FAILED_RULE_IN_BATCH`.

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

When `spark.sql.mapKeyDedupPolicy=LAST_WIN`, have `SimplifyExtractValueOps` visit `CreateMap` entries in reverse order when rewriting a `GetMapValue` lookup into `CaseKeyWhen`. Reverse the key/value pairs together, not the individual expressions. The default `EXCEPTION` path is unchanged.

`CASE` chooses the first matching branch, while `LAST_WIN` requires the last matching map entry. The existing rewrite visits entries in insertion order, so enabling the optimizer changes results.

For example, with `spark.sql.mapKeyDedupPolicy=LAST_WIN`:

```sql
SELECT id, map(id, id, id, id + 10)[id] AS value FROM range(3);
```

The old optimized query returns values `0, 1, 2`; the constructed map requires `10, 11, 12`. A final duplicate entry with a null value is also incorrectly ignored by the old rewrite.

Yes. Optimized map lookups honor the configured `LAST_WIN` semantics, including a last matching value of null. Missing keys and null lookup keys still return null. Queries using the default deduplication policy are not changed by this patch.

pull_requests.title: [SPARK-59805][SQL] Avoid BigDecimal round trips for wide decimals that fit in a long in UnsafeRow
pull_requests.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

For `DECIMAL` columns with precision > 18, `UnsafeRow` stores the unscaled value as big-endian two's-complement bytes. Reading and writing them always went through `BigInteger`/`BigDecimal`, even when the value fits in a `long`:

- `UnsafeRow.getDecimal` allocated a `byte[]`, a `BigInteger`, a `java.math.BigDecimal` and a Scala `BigDecimal` per call, and returned a BigDecimal-backed `Decimal`.
- `UnsafeRow.setDecimal` and `UnsafeRowWriter.write` called `toJavaBigDecimal().unscaledValue().toByteArray()`.

This PR adds a fast path for values whose unscaled value fits in a `long`:

1. `UnsafeRow.getDecimal`: when the stored value is at most 8 bytes, decode it directly from the row into a `long`. If `|unscaled| < 10^18` and `scale <= 18`, return a compact (long-backed) `Decimal` via `Decimal.createUnsafe`; otherwise return the same BigDecimal-backed `Decimal` as before (built with `BigDecimal.valueOf`, without the `byte[]`/`BigInteger`).
2. `UnsafeRow.setDecimal` / `UnsafeRowWriter.write`: after the existing `changePrecision`, a compact `Decimal` is written with the new `UnsafeRow.writeCompactUnscaledBytes`, which emits the minimal big-endian two's-complement bytes of the `long`. These are byte-identical to `BigInteger.toByteArray()`, so the row format, row hashing and row equality are unchanged. Non-compact values keep the existing path.
3. `Decimal.roundToInt`/`roundToShort`/`roundToByte` now truncate exactly via `BigInteger` for BigDecimal-backed values, as `roundToLong` already does, instead of going through a `Double`.

The main effect is on aggregation: the buffer of `sum`/`avg` over `decimal(p, s)` has precision `p + 10`, so e.g. `sum(decimal(15,2))` uses a `decimal(25,2)` buffer. Previously every buffer read came back BigDecimal-backed, so `Decimal.+` never took its existing long fast path; now it does while the running value fits in a long.

### Why are the changes needed?

Performance. The per-row `BigInteger`/`BigDecimal` round trips are a large share of CPU in decimal-heavy aggregations. In a CPU profile of TPC-H SF10, 11.4% of samples were in `java.math.BigDecimal`/`BigInteger` or `Decimal`.

Item 3 is needed for consistency. With the double-based check, a value just below a bound, such as `2147483647.99999999` as `decimal(20,8)`, rounds to `2147483648.0` and `CAST(... AS INT)` wrongly fails with `CAST_OVERFLOW` under ANSI mode. Long-backed values of the same number were already checked exactly. Because this PR returns more wide decimals in the compact form, leaving the double-based check would make the result of the same cast depend on the internal representation.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes, a bug fix. Casting a `DECIMAL` whose value truncates to exactly `Int.MaxValue`/`Int.MinValue` (and likewise for `SMALLINT`/`TINYINT`), but which is close enough to the next integer to round up past the bound as a double, no longer fails with `CAST_OVERFLOW` under ANSI mode (or returns null under `try_cast`). It returns the truncated value, as it already did for the same value held as an unscaled long. For example, `CAST(CAST('2147483647.99999999' AS DECIMAL(20,8)) AS INT)` now returns `2147483647` instead of failing.

No other change: query results, the `UnsafeRow` binary format and plans are unchanged.

### How was this patch tested?

New tests:
- `UnsafeRowWriterSuite`: fixed-seed round trips for precision 19..38 across scales. Values include 0, +-1, +-(10^18 - 1), +-10^18, every byte-length boundary +-2^(8k-1) and its neighbours (including `Long.MinValue`/`Long.MaxValue`), values over 8 bytes, and random values. Each is written through `UnsafeRowWriter` and through in-place `setDecimal`. The tests assert:
  - the row bytes equal a layout built independently from `BigInteger.toByteArray`;
  - `getDecimal` matches the previous BigDecimal-based result in value, precision, scale, `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString`;
  - `toLong`, `toInt`, `roundToLong`, `roundToInt`, `floor` and `ceil` give the same value, or throw the same exception;
  - the result is compact exactly when `|unscaled| < 10^18` and `scale <= 18`.
- `UnsafeRowWriterSuite` also covers rescaling in the writer, and overflow/null handling (null bit set, slot kept, re-update after null).
- `DecimalSuite`: `roundToInt`/`roundToShort`/`roundToByte` on BigDecimal-backed values just inside and just outside each bound, compared with the long-backed representation.
- `DataFrameAggregateSuite`: `sum`/`avg` of `decimal(15,2)` whose running sum crosses unscaled +-10^18 in both directions, grouped and global, with ANSI on and off.

Existing suites pass: `DecimalSuite`, `UnsafeRowWriterSuite`, `UnsafeRowConverterSuite`, `DecimalExpressionSuite`, `ArithmeticExpressionSuite`, `CastWithAnsiOnSuite`, `CastWithAnsiOffSuite`, `TryCastSuite`, `GenerateUnsafeProjectionSuite`, `UnsafeRowSuite`, `DataFrameAggregateSuite`, `MathFunctionsSuite`, and `SQLQueryTestSuite` for the decimal, numeric, cast and try_* inputs. No golden files changed.

Benchmark: a new `DecimalArithmeticBenchmark` (5M rows, 1000 groups; ns per row; ANSI off / on):

| Case | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| sum(decimal(15,2)) | 83.3 / 80.4 | 48.2 / 45.4 |
| avg(decimal(15,2)) | 79.9 / 78.9 | 47.0 / 47.4 |
| sum(p * (1 - d) * (1 + t)), TPC-H q1 expression | 165.9 / 168.6 | 157.6 / 159.2 |
| sum(decimal(28,0)), all values >= 10^18 | 105.8 / 106.3 | 113.7 / 115.6 (within run-to-run noise of about +-5%) |

The q1 expression doesn't improve because the multiply still produces BigDecimal-backed values; that is left for a follow-up. The `*-results.txt` files are not included; they should be generated with the GitHub Actions benchmark workflow.

End to end, TPC-H SF10 (local[4], median of 3 runs) takes 73.8s instead of 79.4s; q1 goes from 11.55s to 8.76s. TPC-DS SF10 is unchanged within noise (its decimals are `decimal(7,2)`, whose sums fit in 18 digits).
